Wine is an emulator. It tries to pretend it is Windows so that the games can believe they are running on Windows. But in reality Wine is running under Linux, so that you, the player can play the game.

Now just imagine that a single person has created Wine, for simplicity's sake. This person needs to program almost the entire Windows operating system again - from mouse and keyboard stuff to graphics, sound, multi-threading and everything else. Except that it's really not that simple because he also has to program everything twice - once for the Windows layer and again for the Linux layer so that when a game sends a sound (for example) to Wine (which the game thinks it's Windows) then Wine can send this sound again to your Linux system so that the Linux system can send it to your headphone or whatever you're using.

I'm simplifying things a bit here but the point is: Wine (and any emulator) is an extremely complex program. They are extremely hard to code. This website estimates Wine would have cost almost 50 million dollars to develop, or around 8 full years if you had a team of a hundred programmers. Sounds about right to me!

So this is why some games work and some don't. Just like big games have plenty of bugs because they are so complex so does Wine. The difference is that sometimes you pay good money for those buggy games while Wine is free. And about why some games run better than others: more popular games (let's say Fallout 2) are better tested and with more people playing more bugs are found and fixes are made in Wine - so when you get to play it everything is already running smoothly. Now obscure games don't have that luxury so chances are that they will be nearly unplayable unless someone is willing to fix whatever bugs come up with it in Wine.

You should look up what the wine acronym means. All snark aside I never really looked into what makes wine not an emulator, but I felt obligated to point that out since somewhere a wine dev is raging every time that is said.

GNU also stands for GNU is Not Unix. Well, technically it isn't but it also technically is.

You can say whatever you want but Wine is a program that executes Windows programs on Linux and this is the exact definition of what an emulator is.

From Wikipedia:

The name Wine initially was an acronym for Windows emulator.

You know what I mean? They may call themselves a compatibility layer to make their implementation method clear but no one is wrong in saying that it emulates the Windows' kernel and DLLs. So it's an emulator, no doubt about it - just not a conventional one.

Yep, I hear you. That's why I neutralized the snark. I finally looked into the not-an-emulator business and quickly found out there's no cpu emulation going on. So by the hardware definition it makes sense, but I fully agree with you, in all other regards it's an emulator.

The name is obviously based on GNU. And GNU says "GNU is not Unix" while what they really mean to say is "we're not Unix, we're actually a Unix clone". Isn't a clone supposed to be the exact same thing as the original? So all in all it's just your typical hacker stuff - pretty clever, overall thought-provoking and somewhat weird and nonsensical, while still making a lot of sense.
